the residues Glu330 and Lys326 of glutamate mutase promote cobalt-carbon homolysis by stabilizing the homolytic product, the adenosyl free radical, and correctly positioning the adenosyl carbon to facilitate the abstraction reaction with the substrate.

the hydrogen bonding interactions between two active site residues (Glu330 and Lys326) and the adenosyl ligand of AdoCbl play a critical role in positioning the coenzyme for efficient hydrogen abstraction from the substrate and in stabilizing the dissociated (homolytically cleaved) state of the coenzyme.

the mechanism of action of a family of enzymes that use adenosylcobalamins (AdoCBLs) as coenzymes.
the role of the protein in promoting homolysis of the cobalt-carbon covalent bond of AdoCbl, a process that occurs in a number of enzymes.
the molecular basis of catalysis by adenosylcobalamins, which is a class of coenzymes that are essential for the biosynthesis of a number of biologically important molecules.

the enzyme's active site residues promote coenzyme homolyses by stabilizing the homolytic transition state and positioning the reactive radical in the correct orientation to react with the substrate.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the active site residues of glutamate mutase play a dual role in catalysis, stabilizing the dissociated state and positioning the adenosyl and substrate groups to promote hydrogen atom transfer.
the protein environment of the AdoCbl coenzyme in the homolytic dissociated state is more favorable for the abstraction of hydrogen than that of the associated state.
the protein can stabilize the homolytlically dissociated coenzyme, but this is not enough to achieve the rate enhancement seen in the enzyme-catalyzed reaction.
